claims.text: The initial Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy is a chemically homogeneous, single-phase, metastable solid solution.
Nonequilibrium processing can produce chemical short-range-order states distinct from equilibrium states.
Thermally activated diffusion during heat treatment drives the development of chemical short-range order in the target alloy.
Chemical short-range ordering triggers nucleation and growth of Mg-rich intermetallic compounds.
Mg-containing multi-principal-element alloys have a tendency to develop intermetallic compounds.
The resulting Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates are fine-scale and form both along grain boundaries and within the matrix.
A fine intermetallic dispersion refines or beneficially modifies grain-boundary characteristics.
Fine Mg-rich precipitates modify the local composition at the oxide-metal interface.
The modified interface enhances protective oxide-film formation and adhesion.
A TiO2-rich surface film can enhance passivation and lower corrosion current density in Mg-Ti-Zn alloys.
A fine and uniform intermetallic dispersion improves or retains corrosion resistance relative to the initial metastable state.
A fine and uniform intermetallic dispersion improves or retains high-temperature oxidation resistance relative to the initial metastable state.
Prolonged or higher-temperature treatment produces coarser intermetallic growth.
Coarse intermetallic phases interrupt the continuity of the protective oxide layer.
Coarse intermetallic growth decreases corrosion resistance.
Coarse intermetallic growth decreases high-temperature oxidation resistance.
The as-cast initial state has a uniform but relatively weak passivating oxide layer.
Temperatures above approximately 150 degrees Celsius define a service-relevant boundary at which precipitation kinetics and oxide-film stability become critical.

contradictions.description: The baseline is declared to be a single-phase solid solution, but the falsification rule asks whether heat treatment produces a significant refinement of intermetallic precipitate size or distribution relative to that baseline. If the baseline has no intermetallic precipitates, refinement relative to it is not a coherent comparison; precipitation or coarsening should instead be assessed.
